This is the leitmotif governing the whole tale, for it states, in veiled language, the secret way out of the cosmic mountain. Most people, of course, will never pass beyond the first two mountains. Others will reach the third, fourth, or fifth, but go no farther.

The third mountain represents the inner, spiritual heaven of the Moon, just beyond the elemental Spheres. Here one already enters the “desert.” This is the deeper meaning of the traditions that tell of the infant Zal abandoned in Alborz; in the present tale the author will simply say “in the desert.” At this boundary, the encounter with the Angel takes place.

If the disciple fails to understand the Angel’s hints, he will indeed get no farther than the third mountain. If he understands them, he will cross them all and reach the Spring of Life. Having become like the drop of balm, he will then have passed from the world of outward, natural appearances to the world of the inward spiritual realities hidden within those appearances, as an almond lies concealed within its shell.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01150

Yet, paradoxically, to pass into the inner world is to find oneself outside—or, in the language of our authors, “on the convex surface of the Ninth Sphere.” That is to say, one finds oneself at the summit of Mount Qaf, and thereby beyond every mountain range. One has left the space of perceptible dimensions by way of the quarta dimensio, the fourth dimension, without needing to “dig a tunnel,” as the questioner naively supposed at the outset. We might think here of knot theory, or of twisting a circular ring into the shape of a figure eight, so that something moving along the inner surface of the eight, from any given point, eventually finds itself on the outside.

II. The second “wonder,” furnishing the second theme of initiation, is the “Jewel That Lights the Night,” a traditional Persian metaphor for the Moon.

But neither here nor in the two following themes are we really dealing with astronomy. To understand what is at stake, it helps to recall a passage in Proclus explaining why Timaeus calls himself “the most astronomical” of the three speakers in Plato’s dialogue bearing his name. Proclus brings in one of the “Chaldean Oracles.” Timaeus, he says, does not describe himself in this way “because he had scrutinized the speeds of heavenly movements or measured the course of the sun by means of a collection of tables … but because he studies the stars above Heaven itself, in accordance with the leader mentioned in the Theaetetus, and contemplates the invisible causes which are stars in the true sense.”

Suhrawardi, too, has these “stars in the true sense” in mind when, for example, in his “Epistle of the High Towers” (Risâlat al-Abrâj), he speaks of Hallaj, Bastami, and other Sufis as “Moons in the heaven of tawhîd”—the realization of divine unity. In that same epistle, written in Arabic rather than Persian, the Moon (qamar, masculine in Arabic) appears as the lover of the queen of the stars, the Sun (shams, feminine in Arabic). The lover never lingers. He presses onward from the lowest point of the new moon to the height of the full moon.

Then, at the fullness of the lunar cycle, the rays of his “queen, the Sun,” are reflected in him, setting his whole being ablaze, though in himself he was nothing but Darkness. Looking within, the lover, stripped of his separate being, can see nothing that is not filled with that light. And so he cries out: “Anâ’l-Shams—I am the Sun!”

Exactly the same lesson appears in the mystical rhapsody “The Language of the Ants,” in its ninth chapter. There we hear the answer the Moon gave to the prophet Idris—whom, as we know, the tradition identifies both with Enoch and with Hermes Trismegistus—when he asked why her light sometimes wanes and sometimes waxes. “Know that my body is dark, but smooth and pure. Of myself I have no light at all.

“Yet when I stand opposite the Sun, and precisely to the degree that I face it, an image of its light falls upon the mirror that is my body, just as the forms of other bodies appear in mirrors […] until, when I look within myself at the moment of encounter, it is the Sun that I see […]. Then, whenever I look at myself, I find that everything is Sun.

“Do you not see that when a mirror is placed before the Sun, the form of the Sun appears in it? If, by divine decree, the mirror had eyes, and looked into itself while facing the Sun, it would find that everything within it was Sun, even though it was made of metal. I am the Sun (Anâ’l-Shams), it would say, because it would see nothing within itself but the Sun. And if it went so far as to say I am God (Anâ’l-Haqq) … even then, we would have to accept its plea in excuse.”

These two passages seem to make any further explanation of the “Jewel That Lights the Night” episode in our tale unnecessary. The Moon represents the mystic journeying through the heaven of tawhîd, divine unity. Her phases represent the successive stages and repeated encounters face to face that bring the mystic’s inner being to a state of incandescence.

At such a moment, the Light that wholly possesses him becomes the active Subject within him. Absorption, or fanâ’, into this Light does not mean the destruction of the mystic’s being or personhood. It means a transformation of consciousness, in which the illusory ego is transfigured in the real Self, the true subject of thought and action. “When my servant draws near to me, I become the eye through which he sees, the ear through which he hears,” and so on.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01160

The more the real Self comes to the fore, the more the lower ego of ordinary consciousness fades and disappears; and the reverse is equally true. This is the meaning of the Angel’s teaching, illustrated by the Moon’s phases, by the little sphere floating on the surface of a bowl, and by the approach to the Tuba tree. Taken to its limit, the second passage quoted above lets us hear the ecstatic declaration of al-Hallaj: Anâ’l-Haqq, “I am God.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01161
But is that, without qualification, the position professed by the Master of Illumination?
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01162

Notice the progression in the two passages just quoted, leading to the final cry: “I am the Sun.” Hallaj’s declaration, “I am God,” appears only as an extreme case. There can be no doubt that the Tuba tree, whose light sets the Moon ablaze, here represents the Sun (compare theme IV)—not, of course, the incandescent body visible in the astronomical heavens, but the “star in the true sense,” the spiritual Sun.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01163

We should therefore return to the psalm dedicated to the Archangel of the Sun (see above, III, section 5). There the author describes that archangel, who is the gateway (pishgâh) to every ecstasy in the spiritual world, as the vicegerent of the Light of Lights. He is its image because it sets him ablaze with its own light. In the present tale we are told, on one hand, where he stands among the eleven mountains: in the fourth Heaven, the Heaven of the Sun, which in Jewish gnosis is the heaven of the Archangel Michael.

On the other hand, we are told that “whoever is familiar with paradise beholds this tree whenever he walks there.” Yet Suhrawardi held, like every spiritual master within Islam, that God Most High and any created being, at whatever level, cannot belong to the same order or species of being. This is precisely the great problem facing these thinkers.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01165

Must we then agree with the rationalist theologians of kalâm, who declare any direct relation between the divine Essence and human nature impossible? Must we assume that such a relation would inevitably mean either a Manichaean “mingling” or the Christian idea of Incarnation? That would be to forget entirely—and the West has forgotten it more than once—the very way forward opened by Shia teaching on the Imam. It is profoundly significant that both the Tuba tree and Simorgh have been understood, in Twelver Shiism and Ismailism alike, as symbols of the Imam.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01166

For the Imam is the Sun, the Face, the Perfect Human Being, the form of divine manifestation (mazhar) who can fill a believer with the Light manifested within himself without dissolving that believer’s created existence. The walâyat of the faithful—their standing as “friends of God”—is a lunar walâyat in relation to that of the Imam. The present tale does not explicitly speak of the Imam; it speaks instead of the Tuba tree and Simorgh.

The Angel’s hint is discreet, given in half-spoken words. Without pressing those words too hard, we may observe that the relation between Moon and Sun in the heaven of the malakût, the world of the Soul, establishes the very conditions of the hikâyat recalled earlier. In that threefold unity, the person telling the tale, the mystical epic, and the one whose deeds are recounted become one. At its limit, the situation finds expression in Anâ’l-Shams: “I am the Sun.” At the end of our tale, the initiate will be called upon to decide whether he can say, “I am Khezr,” and, by that very fact, whether he can cross Mount Qaf.

III. The third “wonder,” and the third theme of initiation, grows directly out of the preceding one. It gives rise to a long exposition of particularly dense and allusive meaning, forming the centre of the entire tale. The Angel’s teaching now concerns the Tuba tree and Simorgh. Mention of the mysterious bird itself leads to an extended digression on two heroes of the Iranian epic: first Zal, then Esfandiyar.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01169

We have just recalled the situs, the symbolic location, of the Tuba tree: at the centre of the mountains making up Mount Qaf and, correspondingly, at the centre—and therefore also at the summit—of the malakût, the world of the Soul, or “paradise.” This symbol recurs throughout the mystical traditions. In Ismaili gnosis it represents the Imam as unconditioned existence (wojûd motlaq). A ray from the light of his knowledge is projected into the nature or substance of every inhabitant of paradise, every faithful follower of the Imam. Traditions shared by the whole of Shiism tell us that the branches of the Tuba tree hang down from the highest region of paradise.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01170

This means that whatever the people of paradise desire appears immediately upon its branches, because for them knowledge, desire, and the effective power to bring something about are simultaneous. Similarly, the statement that one of its branches hangs before the window of every place of prayer in paradise means that all its inhabitants share in the tree, each according to the measure of their desire. This simultaneity is also the law of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. Our text seems to refer us to this understanding, while also making the Tuba tree the symbol of the spiritual Sun of the malakût.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01171

Next comes Simorgh, whose nest is “at the summit of the Tuba tree.” We know that the name of this mysterious bird already occurs in the Avesta as Saena meregha, which eventually became the Persian Simorgh. Since the Avestan form is feminine, and Persian does not distinguish masculine and feminine grammatical gender, we prefer to preserve the feminine form of the Avestan name. The Persian form made possible the brilliant play on words by which Attar brings his great mystical epic, Mantiq al-Tayr, The Language of the Birds, to its conclusion.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01172

The name can be read as sî-morgh, “thirty birds.” Under that name, Attar encodes the double mystery of identity within difference and difference within identity, between the eternal Simorgh and the thirty birds, the only ones among thousands to have completed their long and painful quest. We have already referred to the mystical secret encoded in the name Simorgh (see above, Book I, Chapter VII, section 4).
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01173
Naturally, the interpretation of this symbol varies among the authors in whose works it reappears.

For example, in Shams al-Din Lahiji (d. 918/1506), the commentator on The Rose Garden of Mystery (Golshan-e Râz), the great poem by the celebrated Azerbaijani mystic Mahmud Shabestari (d. 720/1317), Simorgh represents the absolute divine Selfhood. Mount Qaf, where she dwells, is the spiritual reality of the Human Being, the Anthropos. This is the perfect form of divine manifestation (mazhar), the Form through which the divine Being reveals its Names and Attributes.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01175

For the Ismaili commentator on the same mystical poem, Simorgh is the name of the Spirit, and the mountain where she dwells is the body. Since Simorgh names the Spirit, it also names the Imam: the Imam is spiritual truth and resurrection, in contrast to the body, which is the outward letter of the sharî’at, the religious law, within which that truth is presently concealed.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01176

Attar’s understanding offers us the best guidance through Suhrawardi’s difficult text. At first Simorgh appears as the eternal Simorgh: she who cares for Zal, and whose Image carries Esfandiyar away in supreme ecstasy, just as the thirty birds stand overwhelmed before the revelation of Simorgh.

Yet later we learn that the name Simorgh can also designate each Simorgh among a multitude of Simorghs. Here we may recall the celebrated theological conception of the “members”: the World Soul is at once identical with its members and, as a distinct spiritual reality, different from them.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic

In another of Suhrawardi's mystical treatises, appropriately entitled The Incantation of the Simorgh, the prologue describes what happens to each hoopoe when spring comes. It leaves its nest, takes flight toward Mount Qaf, and strips itself of its own feathers with its own beak. Once Mount Qaf has cast its shadow over the bird for a period measured in the time of the Malakut, the spiritual kingdom (compare Quran 22:46: one day with your Lord is equal to a thousand years by your reckoning), the hoopoe becomes a Simorgh, whose song awakens those who sleep.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01179

The Simorgh flies while remaining motionless; it takes flight without crossing any distance; it draws near without traversing any interval. All colors are within it, yet it has no color of its own. Its nest is in the East, yet it is not absent from the West. Everyone is concerned with it, yet it depends on no one. All forms of knowledge arise from this bird's song, as does the sound of every musical instrument. Its food is fire. (More than one feature of this description was taken up by a Christian theologian to describe the dove, the mystical symbol of the Holy Spirit.)
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01180

Here, then, we meet the image of the hoopoe becoming a Simorgh. Its flight in the spring coincides with the moment when Kay Khosrow held the Grail toward the rising sun—the hour of Ishraq, the dawn of illumination. The circumstances in which the lower self is cast off correspond, in turn, to the mystical significance of the moon's phases, when it reaches the fullness of its light on the side facing the Tree of Tuba. This is also the moment when the mystic draws the Grail from its tunic of skin.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01181

The Simorgh feeds only on fire—the fire that is the Grail itself (see above, IV, 5). It thus takes on the attributes of the phoenix mentioned by Wolfram von Eschenbach (see above, IV, 1). Through the Grail, “the phoenix is consumed and reduced to ashes.” Yet life is born anew from those ashes, and the phoenix, having undergone its transformation, reappears in all its splendor.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01182

These details from the prologue are invaluable if we are to understand—or at least begin to sense—the Archangel's answer in The Tale of the Crimson Archangel: only an ignorant person, he says, would dare claim that there is just one Simorgh. On the contrary, a Simorgh is continually descending from the Tree of Tuba to the earth, while the one that was there before disappears. Without this ceaseless coming and going, nothing in this world could continue to exist, for nothing in the visible world can endure without the life-giving influence of the spiritual world.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01183

The suggestion that there are many Simorghs recalls the many birds in Attar's mystical epic: the thirty birds (si-morgh) who reach the presence of the eternal Simorgh. What the Archangel says in Suhrawardi's tale would imply that the eternal Simorgh stands in relation to all these birds as each individual Simorgh stands in relation to the human being to whom it belongs. That, indeed, seems to be the suggestion at the end of the fourth theme.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01184

Within the human being, the Simorgh is the mystical “moon,” whose encounter with the sun sets the human being ablaze like a mirror catching the light. It is the heavenly Self and the protecting Angel, the imperishable Face of that being. It corresponds to the Perfect Nature, which is both the mystic's father and child: it feeds upon the flame of the mystic's Grail, and this feeding requires the human being to die to the lower self. When the burning is complete, the human soul—the hoopoe—has become the phoenix-Simorgh. Rising again from its ashes, it takes flight “in springtime” toward the East, the summit of Mount Qaf.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01185

All this is suggested so delicately, through hints and allusions, that we must not weigh it down with an elaborate argument designed to force it into a rigid system of concepts. Here we have to think in images (compare our remarks above, pp. 194 ff.).
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01186

But if we keep in mind the twofold character of the Simorgh, as Suhrawardi suggests it and Attar develops it, we can begin to understand—still only through hints—the episodes of Zal and Esfandiyar that appear at this point in the tale. For clarity, we shall examine them separately below (§4). Here, above all, the Simorgh takes on the full mystical meaning bestowed on it by Iranian Sufism. By that very fact, the image gives the heroic epic its “Eastern destination.” The deeds of the heroes of the Shahnameh find their fulfillment in a mystical epic.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic

IV. The fourth “wonder” consists of twelve workshops, followed by seven further “workshops,” each presided over by a master. Each of the seven masters also has charge of either one or two of the twelve higher workshops. Behind the language of craftsmen and their guilds, we readily recognize an astronomical symbolism: the twelve signs of the zodiac and the seven planetary heavens, each governed by its Angel. Each planet has two “houses” among the signs of the zodiac, except the sun and moon, which have only one each.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01188

Yet, as we observed earlier when referring to a particularly revealing statement by Proclus, this is not intended as a lesson in astronomy. These are spiritual stars in the heaven of the Malakut. The ultimate meaning of the symbolism is therefore clear: the seventh master (the Angel of the moon) borrows his “robe of honor”—that is, his light—from the fourth master (the Angel of the sun). We are brought straight back to the second theme, the “Jewel That Illumines the Night.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01189

The point is that the “moons” in the mystical heaven, set ablaze like mirrors by the spiritual sun of the Malakut, can exclaim: “I am the sun.” The final sentence leaves no doubt: “As I explained to you in speaking of the Simorgh”—the Simorgh “whose nest is at the top of the Tree of Tuba,” a tree that is itself the symbol of the spiritual sun of the Malakut. This, I believe, makes clear the meaning of the Simorgh that we have tried to bring out in our analysis of the preceding theme.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01190

V–VII. The meaning of the last three themes is almost self-evident. The “coat of mail” is the elemental body, “woven” in the workshops just mentioned. It is the leather sheath, the covering of skin that encloses Kay Khosrow's Grail. The Sword belongs to the Angel of Death. With a single blow it breaks open the coat of mail when that armor has served its purpose. For the uninitiated person, who has not devoted a lifetime to undergoing the ordeal of mystical death, the blow causes unimaginable suffering.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01191

But for someone who has discovered the Fountain of Life and bathed in its waters, the coat of mail has become so supple that the blow of the Sword is no longer felt. Thus the last and seventh “wonder” is precisely this: the “Fountain of Life” in the darkness, reached by the mysterious prophet Khezr (Khidr), companion of the prophet Elijah, or perhaps identical with him. The Archangel's final instructions are intended to initiate his disciple into the search for the Fountain of Life—that is, into the passage through Mount Qaf to its heart or summit. His final words are: “If you are Khezr, you too can pass through Mount Qaf without difficulty.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01192

Once again we hear the image of a drop of balm passing through to the back of a hand heated by the sun, as a piece of iron is made incandescent by fire. “If you are Khezr”: in other words, if the condition of the hikayat, the mystical telling of a tale, is fulfilled, and Khezr is not merely someone whose story the narrator relates from the outside, as an “objective” event. No: in the act of mystical recitation, the narrator, Khezr himself, and Khezr's journey to the Fountain of Life become one and the same reality—as they did in the “Tale of the Grail,” and as they will again in the “Tale of Exile.”

4. From the Birth of Zal to the Death of Esfandiyar
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01193

These episodes may well be the key to the meaning of The Tale of the Crimson Archangel. Yet they may also be the hardest to interpret, because their meaning is deliberately veiled and conveyed through a wealth of allusions.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01194

We may come closest to understanding Suhrawardi's intention if we grasp two motifs together: the soul's “descent” into this world, and the “guardian angel”—the daimon paredros, or agathos daimon (the good or companion spirit)—from whom the soul separates when it descends here, and with whom it is reunited when it leaves this world, “when the hoopoe takes flight in springtime and becomes a Simorgh.” Both motifs are fundamental to Neoplatonic thought. Here doctrine becomes story, and through that story Suhrawardi seeks to suggest the meaning and role of the Simorgh. Its intervention brings the heroic epic of Iran to its fulfillment as a mystical epic. In this way, the undertaking that the Shaykh al-Ishraq, the Master of Illumination, carried within him all his life finds its completion.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01195

He therefore chooses two moments from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh in which the Simorgh's intervention presents an especially compelling mystery for spiritual interpretation. The Archangel tells his listener the soul's spiritual history, from its beginning in this world to its final passage beyond it.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01196

But the material of the Iranian heroic epic divides the drama—the soul's descent into this world and its final ascent back to its own world—between two characters: Zal, the hero of the epic cycle of Sistan, and Esfandiyar, the champion of the Zoroastrian faith. The latter's character was ideally suited to the purposes of the Shaykh al-Ishraq as the “reviver of the wisdom of ancient Persia.” From Zal's birth under the protection of the Simorgh to Esfandiyar's death in the supreme ecstasy that ends his earthly struggle, the mysterious presence of the Simorgh makes itself felt throughout.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01197

It would take us too far afield to collect all the traditions about Zal in the Avesta, Ferdowsi, and the writers of the Islamic period, along with the many interpretations they have received. We need consider only the episode chosen by Suhrawardi: the birth of Zal, father of Rostam, the famous hero of Sistan. In Ferdowsi's epic, Zal appears chiefly as the wise adviser of the Kayanian kings. Earlier in this chapter (IV, 3), we mentioned him as one of Kay Khosrow's eight companions on the journey to the “high mountain.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01198

Yet Zal was among the three who heeded Kay Khosrow's warning, chose not to follow him farther, and found their way back to this world. The extraordinary feature of Zal's birth, recalled by the author of our tale, is familiar throughout the tradition. Suhrawardi, however, seems to have been the first to reveal its hidden meaning.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01199

The disciple's question to the Archangel comes immediately after the description of the Tree of Tuba as the tree “at whose summit the Simorgh has its nest.” We saw how this deepens the preceding theme: the relationship between the “Jewel That Illumines the Night” and that same Tree of Tuba, the spiritual sun at the summit of the Malakut. Recall also the other passage from Suhrawardi cited above: “A Simorgh continually descends from the Tree of Tuba to earth, while the one that was there before disappears.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01200

There are, of course, several ways to unfold the meaning of this image. We have noted, for instance, that a Shiite mystic may read the Simorgh as a hidden symbol of the Imam and the Imamate. The interpretation proposed here seems to me both to make this deliberately veiled text intelligible and to accord with Suhrawardi's overall purpose in his books and tales.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01201

The Simorgh's descent to earth seems to accompany the descent of the human soul. It is the guardian angel, the agathos daimon that, according to Iamblichus, exists as an original model or pattern even before souls descend into the world of becoming (genesis). Plotinus had already said (Enneads IV, 8, 8) that no soul, not even our own, is wholly immersed in the world perceived by the senses: “There is something in it that always remains in the intelligible world. Every soul has a lower side turned toward the body and a higher side turned toward Intellect.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01202

At its furthest reach, this higher soul can be understood as the personal angel who inspires our thoughts and governs our actions—until, as Iamblichus also says, through “sacred theurgy” we entrust the direction and protection of our soul to a god, with the angel acting as that god's assistant. This is, in brief, the figure we identified in an earlier analysis (Chapter III, 1, pp. 88–92): on the one hand, the personal good spirit (agathos daimon) of Hermes and of the Hermetic philosopher, or the “Perfect Nature,” both “father” and “child” of the soul, to which Suhrawardi dedicated his magnificent hymn; on the other, the angel Daena, a sacred manifestation of the Xvarnah, the divine glory of Mazdean wisdom.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01203

In Suhrawardi, the Simorgh seems to occupy this same place. It also corresponds to the Fravarti (foruhar) of Mazdean thought, the heavenly counterpart of an individual living on earth. Although the Simorgh descends with each human soul, it remains distinct from that soul: its original pattern, its counterpart, its heavenly companion. It can therefore be said to care for the soul and watch over it. If the soul has remained faithful to the Simorgh, its supreme moment, the supreme vision at its departure from this world—as in Suhrawardi's interpretation of Esfandiyar—is reunion with the Simorgh, the joining into one of the two who belong together.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01204

“When the hoopoe becomes the Simorgh,” the Simorgh “whose nest is at the summit of the Tree of Tuba,” the tree that entirely bathes it in light, then, in knowing that light, it knows itself. This interpretation would satisfy both the indications Suhrawardi gives us and those of Attar's great epic, in which the thirty birds, the si-morgh, discover that they themselves are the eternal Simorgh.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01205

When the disciple asks whether it is true that the Simorgh raised Zal, the Archangel replies by recounting the circumstances of Zal's birth, familiar from the traditions about him. Zal was born with hair completely white. His father, Sam, was horrified and ordered the child to be abandoned in the wilderness. His mother, equally shaken, either could not or did not know how to oppose the order. It was winter, and no one imagined that the child could survive.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01206

After a time, however, his inconsolable mother went in search of her son and found him in that same wilderness. To her amazement, he was still alive. By day, the Simorgh sheltered him beneath its wings. By night, a gazelle whose fawn had been taken by hunters came to feed him. What secret lay behind this? The Archangel himself had questioned the Simorgh, and received this answer: “Zal came into the world beneath the gaze of Tuba. We did not allow him to perish.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01207

We did not allow him: that is, the Simorgh and the “Tree” of Tuba, at whose summit the Simorgh has its nest. The symbolism of color immediately helps us sense that the whiteness of the infant Zal's hair marks his descent from the world of beings of light, whose color is white. The “crimson” Archangel himself tells the disciple that in his own world he is pure whiteness. More generally, in the color symbolism of Islamic spiritual philosophy—admirably explained, among others, by Qazi Sa'id Qommi—the closer a being's color is to white, the nearer it is to the spiritual world of Light and the more clearly it belongs there.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01208

As the whiteness diminishes, passing through yellow, orange, red, then green, and finally black, the change marks an increasing distance from that world. The very sign of origin carried in Zal's hair both angers and terrifies his father, as if Sam were someone unable to accept such an origin, or someone frightened by the gravity of its consequences. The child is abandoned in the wilderness, just as the traveler in the Tale of Western Exile is thrown to the bottom of a well.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01209

How can a being exiled from the world of Light survive the wilderness and loneliness of this world? How can it avoid the death a soul may suffer through what Plotinus calls “mixture with its opposite”? Yet Zal survives through the watchful care of the Simorgh. We are told that everything which continues to exist in this world does so through the Simorgh. As in the Tale of Exile, we encounter the symbolic alternation of day and night, whose meanings may be reversed according to the context (see Chapter VI below).
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01210

Here the Simorgh watches over Zal by day because day represents the world of Light, the soul's homeland, of which it retains an intuition and of which initiation will one day make it fully conscious. Night, in this case, represents the world of perception confined to the senses. When the symbolism is reversed, day represents the compelling evidence of sense perception, while awareness of the country beyond Mount Qaf requires the senses to fall asleep, to enter their night—as in the Tale of Exile or The Rustling of Gabriel's Wings. Here, by contrast, night is the night of the intellect. That is why it is the gazelle that cares for Zal at night: the gazelle represents the living, sensing soul, the anima sensitiva.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01211

This “history” is the one human beings have known how to tell themselves—and perhaps still know how to tell—when they understand their past not as something reconstructed from the traces, archaeological or paleontological, of their outward existence, but as something that leads them, in person, back to their origin. That origin is as distant and as near today as it was for their predecessors in the remotest imaginable historical past. The tale, the hikayat, is essentially an act of interpretation that brings each teller, anew, to the true meaning of the story for that person, and in the same movement to the true meaning of that person's own being. It is an act of interpretation carried out as a sacred recitation.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01212

We shall see this even more clearly in the Tale of Exile, where verses from the Quran are themselves “recited” in this way. But we can already glimpse it if we recognize the connection with the ancient Greek romance, whose meaning in the mystery religions Reinhold Merkelbach has worked to uncover through close thematic analysis. The descent of the soul into this world, its captivity here, and its eventual release form the theme of a literature so extensive that, brought together as a single body of works, it would stand as a monument and testimony to the soul's “history.” Suhrawardi's mystical tales, and with them the whole cycle of Persian mystical epic, would belong to it.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01213

The “history” told in all these works is the only history a gnostic can truly tell (see Chapter VI, 1 below): the history of someone who knows where they came from and where they are going. Perhaps few people today can understand it, because it concerns events inaccessible to what we now ordinarily call History. It stands in stark contrast to the spiritually devastated and emptied universe of homo oeconomicus, the human being defined by economic life—a universe with no “polar” dimension, no origin and no final spiritual destiny, yet all the more anxious to declare itself “on the right side of history”: a history that is not its own.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01214

We shall consider only two particularly striking examples. First is Longus's romance Daphnis and Chloe, which is connected with the mysteries of Dionysus. Daphnis is the initiate, the son of Dionysophanes—that is, of the god himself. His human parents are merely his foster or adoptive parents. The god has “exposed” him in this world, but does not abandon him here: he arranges a miraculous deliverance. He gives him a token of recognition that will one day establish his divine origin. Like Zal, Daphnis is fed by an animal during the time of his abandonment, in his case a goat. Even the little fawn left to the hunters in Suhrawardi's story has a counterpart in Longus: the ram that saves Daphnis and Chloe from danger, and that they sacrifice as the price of their ransom.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01215

A second echo of Suhrawardi's story in the Greek romance appears in the work of Heliodorus, probably an Arab living in the third century of the Common Era. This is an initiatory romance associated with the cult of Helios, a solar religion that gathered the religions of the ancient world into itself, just as the romance gathered up what earlier stories had created in honor of Isis or Mithras. In this story, Chariclea, daughter of Hydaspes, king of Ethiopia, is born with an entirely white complexion—the counterpart of the white hair of the infant Zal. We are told that during her pregnancy her mother had gazed upon an image of Andromeda, and her daughter was born in Andromeda's very likeness.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01216

Yet the mother is seized by a fear like that of Sam, Zal's father. Why is this child, whose complexion ought to be dark, unlike the others? Will her legitimacy be challenged? Will mother and daughter be condemned to death? For that reason, her mother, Persina, decides to “expose” her—as Daphnis was exposed, as Zal was “exposed in the wilderness.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01217

But she does not send the child away without a few treasures, including a cloth embroidered with hieroglyphs: a letter in which the mother reveals the secret of her daughter's origin, commands her never to forget it, and tells her to shape her life accordingly. We shall return later to this image of the “letter.” For now, notice that Andromeda, chained to a rock and seemingly defenseless before the dragon from which Perseus will rescue her, is herself the very image of Psyche, likewise chained to a rock.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01218

Thus Chariclea, a new Andromeda, represents—as does the infant Zal—the fate of every human soul cast into this world and bound here, forgetting its divine ancestry until initiation awakens that knowledge. Its true homeland is the mystical land of the sun, the “East,” and all its striving must be directed toward returning there. This is the “East” in Suhrawardi's sense: the destination set before the disciple of the “Crimson Archangel,” and the destination reached at the end of Suhrawardi's Tale of Western Exile, just as it is reached at the end of the Hymn of the Pearl in the Acts of Thomas (see Chapter VI below).
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01219

Other examples could surely be cited in which an Iranian hero appears specifically in a Greek initiatory romance. But the examples we have placed around the story of Zal's birth already confirm the hidden meaning that Suhrawardi asks the spiritual seeker to discover. They also prepare us to understand the hidden meaning of Esfandiyar's death, the second half of this paired picture.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01220

The protection of the soul cast into the world and the release of that soul are both the work of the Simorgh. Its protection is clear in the episode of Zal's birth. Its work of deliverance is less obvious in the course of Zal's later life, despite the protection it has promised him. Or rather, for Suhrawardi's purpose, even if the Simorgh continues to assist Zal, and even if Zal and his son appear to benefit from that assistance, its true beneficiary is another: the young Esfandiyar, who dies after a heroic battle in a final vision of the Simorgh, a vision the Simorgh itself prepares for him through Zal's intervention.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01221

Above all, we must remember that in mystical language “to perish” always has reference to the other world. One does not “perish” to this world, because this world is precisely what it means to “perish” to the true world. Just as the Simorgh did not allow the child with the luminous hair to “perish,” it did not allow Esfandiyar to “perish,” although from an outward perspective it might appear otherwise. In truth, the one who perishes is Rostam. This, it seems to us, is Suhrawardi's spiritual interpretation of the episode from the Shahnameh.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01222

To understand it, we must recall a little of the traditional story. Throughout his life, Zal retains the protection of the Simorgh. When they parted, it gave him one of its feathers, telling him that in distress or danger he need only burn a portion of it “to see the splendid being appear.” Yet the Zoroastrian religious tradition viewed Zal and his famous son Rostam with some reserve, because neither had been eager to accept Zoroaster's preaching.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01223

By contrast, the young Esfandiyar is the very model of a knight of the Zoroastrian faith. According to the epic tradition, the immediate causes of his death cast something of a shadow upon his father, King Goshtasp (Vishtaspa in Avestan). The king supposedly compelled his son to undertake ever more difficult feats in order to postpone the day when he must fulfill his promise to hand over the throne.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01224

Esfandiyar is eventually forced to make an impossible demand of Rostam, who resists the new faith: nothing less than that Rostam submit to being led in chains to the court of King Goshtasp. Rostam tries every possible way of reaching an agreement, but Esfandiyar cannot consent. At last the two heroes agree to settle the war through single combat, whose outcome can only be tragic. The brave Rostam is grieved at having to fight a young hero he admires; the sentiments on both sides remain entirely chivalrous. The battle goes badly for Rostam. He cannot prevail, and, seriously wounded, he is about to die.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01225

Then, according to the epic, his father Zal appeals to the Simorgh. The bird appears, heals Rostam's wounds, and says that an agreement would be best. The Simorgh can certainly make Rostam victorious; but he must know that whoever takes Esfandiyar's life can expect happiness neither in this world nor in the next. Rostam does not consider this price too high. During the night the Simorgh therefore carries Zal to the shores of China, to a tamarisk tree. Following his guide's instructions, Zal cuts off a branch and fashions from it an arrow with two points.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01226

Suhrawardi knew these details of the heroic tradition. Yet his tale now draws upon another source of knowledge: information that the Archangel tells his listener he has received from the Simorgh itself. This new knowledge has the power, by that very fact, to transform the past, to “break open history.” The Simorgh now seems to arrange everything so that Zal, its protégé, can both save his son Rostam from physical death and ensure that Esfandiyar, beneath the appearance of defeat, achieves the triumph of a death in ecstasy.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01227

Through the Simorgh's care, the Iranian hero's story acquires its mystical conclusion. Simply comparing the two accounts allows us to see, almost as it happens, the elevation of meaning accomplished by spiritual interpretation. The heroic tradition says that Esfandiyar was vulnerable only in his eyes. Rostam therefore had to strike him there to inflict a mortal wound. But now that vulnerability takes on a higher meaning: it becomes the vulnerability of inward vision. For there can be an inner vision so overwhelming that it carries the seer out of this life in a supreme ecstasy.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01228

Here we should recall the theory of mirrors and forms of manifestation in the “Eastern theosophy,” the philosophy of illumination, where the Shaykh al-Ishraq describes what we might call the laws of a spiritual optics—the conditions under which visionary perception becomes possible. Certain surfaces with the properties of mirrors can serve as the place where a form beyond the senses, belonging to the imaginal world, becomes visible (a mazhar, a place of manifestation). This does not mean that the form is contained within the mirror. It does not become embodied there; it is not inside it. It is present there “in suspension,” as the image of a person appears in a mirror placed before them.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01229

Moreover, this form is perceived not through the external senses but through the imaginative faculty. Seen in this light, the details reported by the Archangel—those that explain the precautions Zal takes—become clear. The Simorgh possesses this power: if a mirror, or some other polished surface, is held directly before it, every “eye” that looks into the mirror is dazzled. (Recall Kay Khosrow holding the Grail, the mirror of the universe, toward the sun at the spring equinox, the season when the hoopoe takes flight to become a Simorgh.) This is why Zal dresses his son Rostam in shining armor and a gleaming helmet, and covers his horse completely with pieces of mirror.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01230

When Esfandiyar necessarily comes face to face with Rostam in battle, the Simorgh's rays strike the armor and mirrors and are reflected into Esfandiyar's eyes, dazzling him. The two points of the tamarisk arrow wound his eyes mortally. He believes his eyes have been wounded because he has seen the arrow's two points. But what Esfandiyar actually sees with his inner sight is the two wings of the Simorgh.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01231

We find ourselves once again in the situation encountered at the end of the “Tale of the Grail,” and to be encountered at the end of the next tale when its author exclaims, “It is I whom this story is about.” This is the situation of the hikayat, the mystical recitation, in which the deed recounted, the hero whose deed it is, and the person who recounts it form a threefold unity—one reality. More precisely, this unity is brought to completion at the end of the tale, when the Archangel tells his disciple: “If you are Khezr, then you too can cross Mount Qaf.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01232

In that case, the initiate is the story being told. That person is one of the many Simorghs mentioned in our tale, just as each is one of the thirty birds, the si-morgh, in Attar's magnificent epic. This reveals the mystical meaning of Esfandiyar's death. The Simorgh that nests in the Tree of Tuba at the summit of Mount Qaf is the divine Face as it appears to the human being; at the same time, it is that human being's own imperishable Face, the Iman or Angel of their being.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01233

In this meeting face to face, the two Faces reflect one another and answer one another. A human being may glimpse this vision in advance, but cannot go beyond it without crossing the threshold. For certain apparitions always announce that the other world is near: “Whoever sees me bids farewell to the daylight of this life. You have seen the burning gaze of the Valkyrie. Now you must depart with her.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01234

In this central episode of The Tale of the Crimson Archangel, the heroic epic of Iran reaches its fulfillment as a mystical epic. This is entirely in keeping with the purpose of the Shaykh al-Ishraq's “Eastern theosophy”—not only the work to which he devoted his life, but the meaning that the philosophy of Ishraq was to have for the whole spiritual life of Islamic Iran. In the opening chapters of this second book, we described Suhrawardi's undertaking as a return of the so-called “Hellenized” Magi to their original homeland, Iran—but an Iran that had, in the meantime, heard the call of the Prophet of Islam.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01235

The completion of Iran's heroic epic as a mystical epic is thus one aspect of the transformation through which the wisdom of the sages of ancient Persia passes, so that it can find itself at home once again in the Persia of Suhrawardi and his successors. For Zoroastrian tradition, Esfandiyar's death was the work of Ahriman's demonic powers, acting through those who resisted the faith of Zoroaster. Now the spiritual interpretation—the ta'wil—of an Iranian Muslim mystic drives out Ahriman's demons, rescues the heroes from their grasp, and gives Esfandiyar's death the meaning our tale suggests.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01236

One of our earlier publications was illustrated with an extraordinary image published some twenty years ago by Gaston Wiet. It is woven into a silk textile found in 1925 in a tomb near Tehran, perfectly preserved. What makes it especially fascinating is that a motif in the Sasanian style appears on a textile from the early Islamic period, forming an artistic link between ancient and Islamic Persia. A young man, his royal hair forming something like a halo, is being carried aloft by a great fantastic bird that holds him against its breast. Certain stylized details suggest that the bird is not simply a two-headed eagle, but the Anqa (phoenix) or Simorgh. We naturally think of Zal, son of Sam, carried away and nourished by the Simorgh.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01237

Yet an image remains an image, and its meanings are inexhaustible for anyone who meditates on it, because they extend beyond the conscious intentions of the artist who made it. We have therefore suggested that one may discern in it a theme of individual destiny beyond death, well known in Islamic mysticism. In the present context, the Simorgh's intervention at the end of Esfandiyar's earthly life invites us to see in the Iranian artist's solemn image of ascent into heaven the fate of the hero whom the Simorgh bears skyward in a movement of apotheosis.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01238

The purpose of the preceding pages has been to lead us to a translation of The Tale of the Crimson Archangel, which we can now offer without adding further notes. Our interpretation, of course, has by no means exhausted the tale's possible meanings.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01239

But symbols cannot be “refuted.” Either we understand them or we do not. Different interpretations merely occupy different levels of understanding. Each reader must choose the level at which to stand.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic

‘At the beginning of things, when the One who is the Maker in the truest sense wished to bring my as yet nonexistent being into existence, He created me in the form of a falcon. In the country where I then lived, there were other falcons. We spoke with one another, listened to one another's words, and understood one another perfectly.’
